name: Dana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm stock manager at Bramley Farm, 200 suckler cows and their calves, which we finish for beef, plus about 150 hectares we cut for hay and silage. Mornings I check the cows, especially at calving, then it's feeding, moving groups, weighing calves. In summer I'm on the mower and the baler most evenings. I use AI every day, for the herd records, to plan grazing, even to price hay when I sell the extra.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is a calf getting up and finding the teat in the rain, and knowing I helped that cow through. The hardest is the money. I'm paid less than the job's worth, I've got about two weeks' savings, and I live in a static caravan on the farm to keep costs down. My dad ran his own haulage firm, so I grew up believing you work hard, you pay your own way, and you don't wait for anyone to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I like my tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a good helper, not a miracle. It saves me time on records and grazing plans, and that's worth something. But cattle still need a person in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep pushing it as far as it goes. If everyone else thinks it's a bust, there's an edge in being the one who still uses it well. My real worries would still be beef prices and my thin bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using AI for records, grazing and selling hay, and start a small side business baling and selling hay to horse owners online. I'd ask the owner for a share of the hay profit instead of a raise. And I'd keep living in the caravan till I'd saved a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of itch to do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a share of the hay profit rather than a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather earn it than ask for it. If I sell more hay, we both win. That's fairer than him just handing me more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does faith fit into your work, if at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly. I say a prayer at calving when it's going badly, and I go to church when the cows let me. It keeps me steady when the bank balance doesn't.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out a good helper, not a miracle, saving time on records and grazing plans. Cattle still need a person in the field.
S0.think: I'd keep pushing it, because there's an edge in using it well when others think it's a bust. My real worries would still be beef prices and my thin bank balance.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for herd records, grazing and hay sales and starts a side business selling hay to horse owners online. Asks the owner for a share of hay profits rather than a raise and keeps living in her caravan to save a deposit.
S0.feel: Calm, with an itch to do more.
S0.quote: I'd rather earn it than ask for it.
S0.fieldNote: Dana combines heavy AI use with a strongly self-reliant, traditional outlook shaped by her father's haulage firm. She prefers profit-sharing to a raise because it feels earned. Faith appears quietly, as a steadying habit. She would see an edge in sticking with AI even if others gave up on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's where I'd want to be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for hardworking people to get ahead if they learn the new tools. I wouldn't want the government slowing it down with rules. But I'd say employers should train their people, not just replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. If robots can feed, bale and monitor the herd, someone has to manage all of it, and I'm already halfway there. The risk is money, because buying kit on finance with two weeks' savings is a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the robot feeders and baling systems inside out and offer to run them for Bramley Farm. I'd look at buying a second-hand robotic mower on finance and doing hay contracting for small farms nearby. I'd keep my outgoings low by staying in the caravan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous about the finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our relief stockman, Pete, who's sixty and does weekends. He's brilliant with cows and hopeless with screens. I'd want the owner to keep him on for calving at least, because no robot knows a cow like Pete does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no government rules slowing it down. Would you want any help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe cheap loans for young farmers buying kit. That's not a handout, it's a hand up, you pay it back. I'd take that.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for hardworking people to get ahead if they learn the new tools, and government shouldn't slow it with rules. Employers should train their people, not just replace them.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because someone has to manage robot feeders and balers and I'm already halfway there. The risk is buying kit on finance with two weeks' savings.
S1.do: Learns robot feeders and baling systems inside out and offers to run them for the farm. Considers buying a second-hand robotic mower on finance for hay contracting and keeps costs low by staying in the caravan.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a little nervous about the finance.
S1.quote: That's not a handout, it's a hand up, you pay it back.
S1.fieldNote: Dana sees opportunity and wants to move early, which is unusual alongside her thin savings. Her line between a handout and a loan she repays is central to her values. She worried about an older relief stockman and wants him kept for calving. She is wary of regulation but not of help she can pay back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hurt a lot of people and we need to look after each other. I'd still say people should learn the new tools fast. And I'd say families and churches will matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the hay contracting idea is dead, because big companies would sell complete systems. Bramley might keep one person to oversee the robots, and it might be me, but just as likely not. With two weeks' money, I'd be exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd forget any finance on kit and save every penny. I'd push hard to be the person who oversees the robots at Bramley, and learn the systems before they arrive. If that failed, I'd go back home and work with my dad, maybe helping his haulage firm through its own changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, tipping into alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no time to build anything of my own. All I can do is grab the one job left and hope it's mine. With five or ten, I'd be the one selling the robots' services, not begging to watch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, but it would sting. I'd try family first, then church, and only then the government. My dad would say the same.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to hurt a lot of people and we need to look after each other, while still learning the new tools fast. Families and churches will matter more than ever.
S2.think: I think the hay contracting idea dies because big companies would sell complete systems. The farm might keep one person to oversee the robots, maybe me, maybe not, and with two weeks' money I'd be exposed.
S2.do: Drops any plans to finance kit and saves every penny. Pushes to be the one who oversees robots at the farm and learns the systems early, otherwise moves home to work in her father's haulage firm.
S2.feel: Anxious tipping into alarmed, praying a lot more.
S2.quote: I'd be the one selling the robots' services, not begging to watch them.
S2.fieldNote: Two years turns Dana from an early mover into someone fighting for the single remaining job. She would take government help only after family and church, and said it would sting. Her father's business offers a fallback. Her faith becomes more visible under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but I can work with tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who work hard to get ready. I'd encourage young farmers to learn the systems now. I'd also say employers owe their people a fair chance to be part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me about three good years of hay contracting with robots before the big players squeeze small operators out. That's enough to save a real cushion and maybe buy a bit of land or a share in some cattle. After that, I'd have to adapt again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd buy a second-hand robotic mower on finance and start contracting for four or five small farms. I'd keep living in the caravan and put half the contracting money aside. By year three, I'd look at buying a small block of land or a share in cattle with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited. Like driving a full trailer down a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd borrow with two weeks' savings. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But my dad started his haulage firm with one lorry and a loan, so I've seen it work. I'd only borrow what I could pay back from two jobs a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why land or cattle, if robots can farm it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whoever owns the land and the cattle still gets paid, even if robots do the work. I'd rather own a bit of the field than be the one replaced in it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for hardworking people to get ready, and young farmers should learn the systems now. Employers owe their people a fair chance to be part of it.
S3.think: I think five years gives me about three good years of robotic hay contracting before big players squeeze small operators out. That's enough to build a cushion and maybe buy land or a share in cattle.
S3.do: Buys a second-hand robotic mower on finance in year one and contracts for small farms, saving half the earnings while living in the caravan. Looks to buy a small block of land or a share in cattle with her father by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but excited, like driving a full trailer down a steep hill.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a bit of the field than be the one replaced in it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Dana turns into an investor, not just a worker, aiming to own land or cattle so she benefits from automation. She is open about the risk and anchors it in her father's example of starting with one lorry and a loan. Her free-market outlook shows clearly. She sets a sensible limit on borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Now that's an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready, so no excuses. Young people should learn the tools and older farmers should be helped to pass on what they know. I'd be cheerful about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do really well with ten years. I'd build the contracting business, save, buy a little land and some cattle, and be running my own small farm with robots by the end. My only worry is getting too greedy and borrowing too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start contracting with one second-hand robot mower and keep the stock job. I'd save hard and stay in the caravan another two years. By year five I'd aim to buy a small farm, with my dad's help on the deposit, and run it with robots and one or two good people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It feels like a future I could build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd finally have time to meet someone. Right now it's cows, hay and church, and that's not much of a social life. If the robots do the late baling, I might be free on a Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want working alongside you on that farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, if he's still going, and a young apprentice. I'd want someone who knows cows and someone who's learning. That's how it should work.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready, so no excuses. Young people should learn the tools and older farmers should be helped to pass on what they know.
S4.think: I think I'd do really well, building the contracting business and owning a small farm run with robots by the end. My only worry is getting greedy and borrowing too much.
S4.do: Starts contracting with one second-hand robot mower while keeping her stock job and stays in the caravan two more years to save. Aims to buy a small farm by year five with family help on the deposit and run it with robots and a couple of people.
S4.feel: Calm and excited about a future she could build.
S4.quote: If the robots do the late baling, I might be free on a Saturday night.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Dana sees herself as a small farm owner using robots, with a clear plan and timeline. Her worry is her own ambition, not the technology. She would still keep an older stockman and an apprentice. A personal life only appears in this longer scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to build anything and I'd be fighting for one job with two weeks' savings. What would help is cheap loans for young farmers to buy kit, not handouts, and employers giving their own people the first chance to run the new systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who ends up owning the land. If robots farm it, the people who own the land and the herd will do fine, and everyone else won't. I'd want young farmers to have a fair shot at owning some.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own a bit of the field than be the one replaced in it.
portrait: Dana Mensah is 27 and stock manager on a 200-cow suckler beef farm with hay ground, living in a static caravan on the farm with about two weeks of savings. She uses AI every day and is keen to move early, but she believes in paying her own way, as her father did with his haulage firm, and leans on faith and family before government. In the slower scenarios she plans robotic hay contracting and, eventually, owning land or cattle; in the two-year picture she is reduced to fighting for the one remaining job. Her central idea is ownership: own part of the field rather than be replaced in it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have no time to build anything and would be fighting for one job with two weeks' savings.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for young farmers to buy kit, not handouts, and employers giving their own staff first chance to run new systems.
